newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers break off talks, protest continues.
newsitem.headline: French truckers break off talks, protest continues.

text.p: Striking French truck drivers and their bosses broke off talks early on Tuesday with little progress on lifting roadblocks which kept freight shipments at a standstill and threatened petrol supplies.
On the ninth day of the protest, union officials said it was growing in strength and putting greater pressure on the economy in the most serious labour unrest in France this year.

The national traffic information centre reported 166 blockades on roads across France at dawn on Tuesday, and truckers sealed off several petrol depots including one in Grigny south of Paris, which supplies ninety percent of petrol sold in hypermarkets in the capital and surrouding region.
The fifth round of talks ended at 6.30 a.m. (0530 GMT) and unions said the little progress which had been achieved was insufficient to justify loosening the screw.
"The truckers must make themselves heard a bit more so that the bosses and the government make a few more concessions," Alain Renault of the Communist CGT union told reporters.
Bosses and unions reached agreement on sick leave and travel expenses, and made progress on union rights, the pro-Socialist CFDT union said.

Union and companies both said that the ball was in the government's camp as it had to take on funding of retirement at 55 rather than 60, one of the truckers' demands alongside higher wages and shorter working hours.
Haulage companies reportedly refused to consider a wage rise. Talks will resume at three p.m. (1400 GMT).
Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said the government was ready to help meet some of the drivers' key demands by facilitating early retirement and reducing payroll taxes.
"The state is ready to take responsibility, in particular by facilitating an agreement on cessation of activities and by contributing to reducing social charges," he told RTL radio.

"I think everyone is well aware that there is no interest in extending the dispute to other sectors. It certainly isn't in the interest of road haulage employees, because some of their demands are legitimate," he said after several other unions threatened to jump onto the truckers' bandwagon.

The national traffic information centre counted 171 blockades on roads across the country. Among new roads targetted were the A31 motorway between Nancy and the Luxembourg border, and the A4 motorway east of Reims.

In Normandy, all petrol depots and refineries near Rouen, including Royal Dutch Shell and Total, were sealed off. Other blockades let cars through to the Pont de Normandie and at the P&O ferry terminal in Le Havre.
Truckers prevented Rouen rubbish collectors from leaving their depot and rubbish in the city went uncollected.
In certain regions including the Pas-de-Calais in northern France, local officials have since Monday imposed rationing of petrol supplies to private car-owners to avert possible shortages.
Force Ouvriere union leader Marc Blondel has threatened to extend the strike to rail and air transport unless a deal was reached by Tuesday.

The CGT called on its members to widen their protests with a national day of demonstrations and rallies at the roadblocks on Wednesday, and five rail unions urged their members to support the strikes "with the appropriate means".
Truckers blocked Channel ports and German border crossings and tightened their noose on oil refineries and fuel depots after earlier all-night talks ended in deadlock on Monday.
Gaullist deputy Patrick Devedjian urged the government to "speed things up" to engineer a quick solution, saying an extension of the strike could paralyse many sectors.

Trade unions announced plans for a 24-hour strike at state-owned utilities Electricite de France and Gaz de France on December 3, and for a two-day strike at Air France and other French airlines on Wednesday and Thursday.
